#6751. Aryna Sabalenka, Coco Gauff, Mirra Andreeva, and More on Winning, Losing, Living, and Dreaming

Ahead of the season-ending WTA Finals tournament, kicking off Sunday at Indian Wells, the world’s eight highest-ranked women’s tennis players gathered for a fashion shoot and an easy hang. There, they talked exclusively to Vogue about their biggest wins, their toughest losses, their secret lives away from the court (pole dancing, UFC, baking cakes—who knew?)—and what they like to wear.

HEATED RIVALRY? Elina Svitolina, in Tom Ford, scores a snack while Rybakina, Gauff, and Muchova come away empty-handed.

The Indian Wells final was one of the best, because it was a really tough match, and I was a couple of match points down—I had to overcome a lot of things, and I got the win.

Obviously the Australian and US Open finals—in Australia [against Elena Rybakina], I had a break in the third set and felt like everything was going my way, but then it slipped, so I was really, really disappointed with that one. I should have won that one, but I didn’t. The US Open, not so much—[Rybakina] played really incredibly, and I didn’t.

When you walk out onto the court for a match, you’ve got headphones on. What are you listening to?

Sometimes nothing—sometimes I just like to block out the noise and stay in my thoughts. Sometimes I just put on some melodies that make me feel fired up. It’s always different—it just depends on my mood. I have a lot of favorite artists. I like Beyoncé. I like Rihanna. I like Dua Lipa, Tate McRae, Teddy Swims, Eminem, Justin Timberlake, 50 Cent, Britney Spears. I just need to rotate.

If you didn’t play any sport, what would you do for a career?

I think boxing or modeling—they’re so different, but both are things that I love.

Is there a sport other than tennis that you watch or play?

In Dubai—it’s actually crazy to say—but for the first time in my life I went to watch a UFC fight, and I became obsessed. I’m watching lots of fights now, and my entire algorithm is UFC and fighters. I became a huge fan of Khabib [Nurmagomedov, the undefeated UFC legend]. So, yeah, I’m crazy about UFC. I also like ice hockey, and I like to watch basketball and Formula One. I’d like to watch more MotoGP, but I cannot watch it because I’m like, How do you guys do that? It’s so dangerous. I feel so tight watching them race—I’m so scared for them.

I know that you like to get dressed up and that you’re no stranger to going big. You like a big heel, yeah?

Well, I love the way my body looks. But walking, as an athlete? It’s like a workout for me. I had to walk Vogue World in Milan, and I was just dying, because I’m not used to walking in high heels. But still, that was the best experience of my life.

Probably the US Open. I won the Australian Open at the beginning of the year, but the US Open just felt a little bit bigger this year, and New York is such a special city.

What’s your best weapon on the tennis court?

Just the aggressive style of my game. My serve can put me in a position where I can attack from the first ball and be dominant from the beginning of the point, and when that works, it doesn’t really matter who is on the other side.

When you’re away from the court, do you have a guilty pleasure, an indulgence, or a hobby?

I love sweets. With all the travel, I’m very sensitive, so it’s really not easy for me to just let it go and eat whatever I want, but yeah. When I get a chance, I kind of destroy myself—not just sweets, but everything baked: croissants, pain au chocolat.

HOLDING COURT From left: Karolina Muchova in Balenciaga. Sabalenka in a Nike jacket and Gucci skirt and shoes, Comme Si socks. Linda Noskova wears Missoni shorts and a jacket and white leather trench by The Frankie Shop; Miista boots. Pegula wears Chanel.

I played a really great match against Amanda [Anisimova] in Australia to make the semis, and then winning the Dubai title—being able to beat [Elina] Svitolina in the final—was really great. Everyone knows Dubai, and it’s cool to say, “Oh yeah, I won that title in Dubai.” I also played a really great match against Iva Jovic to make the quarterfinals in Wimbledon. I felt like I was able to go up two levels and kind of take the match from her, and to be able to do that against a younger player in a big situation felt great.

Did you have a hero or role model when you were growing up?

I didn’t watch a ton of tennis growing up—I was playing tennis—but my mom read me a lot of books about players, biographies and autobiographies, and I remember being drawn to Martina Hingis and Mary Pierce when my mom would read me their stories.

What’s your best weapon on the tennis court?

I’m very good at staying even-keeled and not wasting a lot of energy. It drains me when I’m wasting a lot of emotional energy. Some people play off of that and can handle it great, but I feel that gives me too many ups and downs.

One piece of advice for an average club player?

Sometimes I think people see pro players hit the ball and they’re like, Oh—I need to hit it harder. And you absolutely do not. I think that learning how to hit your medium rally ball that you can make 85% of the time is really important, because that’s something you can build your game around.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

I used to meditate quite a bit, and I feel like I can always go back to it if I’m feeling a nervous or anxious type of energy. Then I move on to just focusing on breathwork, which I think is so important for us when we’re on the court, too. Sometimes if you focus on your breath and let everything else just kind of happen, everything starts flowing and you get more instinctual, which I think is how you always want to play.

Do you have a guilty pleasure or something that you indulge yourself in when you’re away from tennis?

I play a lot of Call of Duty. Hours. I have a gaming laptop and I have a PS5 at home. One of my best friends and her boyfriend play, and my husband and I play with them all the time. I play with my brother and my sister a lot, too. I was a big Sims kid—sometimes I’ll whip that out and play for three days straight and then put it away for a year—and I went through a big Grand Theft Auto phase. I’ve heard mixed things about the new GTA—people are questioning the graphics—but let’s just say I’m interested.

If you didn’t play tennis—or any sport—what kind of job would you have?

When I was younger, I got really into hockey and always said that I wanted to be the first female GM of a hockey team. But now that I know too much, being a GM sounds really stressful.

When you’re getting dressed for a big night out, do you have a favorite piece, or something that you love that’s important to you?

I like traveling with a good dress and then elevating that with nice shoes or a purse or a jacket. And I’m definitely a jewelry person—that’s always been my thing.

You’re wearing Chanel here—were you a fan before this?

I got a really nice Chanel bag that I wore throughout my whole wedding weekend a few years ago, and I have a really nice pair of Chanel shoes, and another Chanel bag in a [Buffalo] Bills kind of blue that I’ve worn to games.

The Rome title—I had won there before twice, but winning there again as a mom, eight years later, was really a proud moment.

Did you have a hero or a role model growing up?

I really loved watching Andre Agassi—I loved his style of play and his presence on the court, and as a young player I always tried to imitate him, in a way: his spirit, his energy, the way he created the game on his own terms.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

Over the years, I’ve tried different tactics: Sometimes meditation works for me, sometimes it’s watching motivational videos, sometimes music—AC/DC, Eminem, Red Hot Chili Peppers. I also really love the spirit of Kobe Bryant and the way that he kind of went into this state.

Yeah, exactly—he was just really focused on the goal, the mission.

If you didn’t play any sport, what kind of job do you think you would have?

I would be a chef. Cooking really brings me joy, and when I’m home, I like to cook for the family. My grandmother and my mom are great cooks—I think it’s in our culture to prepare something nice.

CHEERING SECTION Clockwise, from top left: Pegula, Svitolina, Noskova, and Muchova are all gunning for number-one.

I mean, you don’t have to, but if I were you I probably would.

Yeah. From any perspective, that final was mentally and physically one of the toughest matches that I’ve ever played in my life.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

I usually like to calm down—I don’t really like to do anything right before my match, like listen to music or whatever, but a few hours before that I like to read: horror, something historical, a biography. I like a lot of different genres.

Do you have a guilty pleasure or something that you indulge yourself in when you’re away from tennis?

In my off-season, I like to travel to different places to see different cultures, different people, different languages. Last year I went to Zanzibar, in Tanzania, and volunteered at a local kindergarten for a week or 10 days, which was short but sweet, and I would love to go back there again.

Is there a sport other than tennis that you either watch or play?

I’ve been a huge fan of WWE since I was 14 or 15. It’s pretty weird for a European kid—I watched it on YouTube, but then when I was in America for the first time I put on some random channel and saw the wrestling and I was super pumped about it. That was my first time watching it live. I love Charlotte Flair, Sasha Banks, and some men as well, like the Undertaker and John Cena. Charlotte Flair was in my player’s box at the US Open this year—she’s obviously super strong and such an athlete, but at the same time, she’s a gorgeous woman, and so cool.

The finals in Doha—and playing doubles with Serena [Williams, in Berlin] was also so important, even if we lost in the first round. But it was a special match—just to have the chance to stand with such a champion as Serena and to practice with her.

What’s your best weapon on the tennis court?

My creativity—the way I can make the court very uncomfortable for my opponents…and for myself, sometimes, too.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

I listen to songs—different ones at every tournament. It can even be a slow song that brings you some feelings, but I always play that one song, and then I’m over it and go to another one. Lately it’s been just beats, fast songs, but it can be something from Beyoncé or Harry Styles, or some Czech pop songs.

Do you have a guilty pleasure or something that you indulge yourself in when you’re away from tennis?

I eat crazy food. I have a sweet tooth, so candy, chocolate, ice cream, pancakes; but I also like junk food, hamburgers, and everything that I can’t have when I play. I also play guitar—just to relax, as a hobby. I’ve been playing for about nine years, both acoustic and electric. I have a beautiful Takamine acoustic and a really nice Fender Stratocaster that my parents gave me for my birthday this year.

Is there a sport other than tennis that you watch or play?

My dad and my brother are both footballers—my dad is now a coach—so I watch Czech football, and when I’m in America I like to go watch the NBA or NHL.

When you’re getting dressed for a big night out, do you have a favorite piece, or something that you love that’s important to you?

I like to have a nice bag and jewelry, but overall I’m going for effortless and casual. I like simple pieces that look like I didn’t try too hard to put them together, even if I actually did.

SHINE ON Sabalenka, Gauff (wearing Tacori earrings and bracelets), Rybakina (wearing Tacori necklace and earrings) , and Mirra Andreeva (in Chanel) take to the stands instead of the court.

Probably the US Open quarterfinal against Mirra [Andreeva]—I saved two match points. I wasn’t really playing that well, but I fought really hard for that one. I also think the energy in New York just gives you an extra motivation to go the extra mile and never give up. And I’m always not giving up, but sometimes home court advantage is a thing.

Did you have a hero or a role model growing up?

The Williams sisters—Serena and Venus—are definitely my idols. Still are. Just seeing a woman of color dominating a sport that didn’t always cater to them historically. Also, their ability at merging sports, fashion, and culture is something that I always was interested in.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

Usually I try to meditate a little bit—I try to visualize myself just being successful in the match and seeing myself doing successful things. After that, honestly, I’m just on TikTok or just being normal.

Yes—usually some hype rap music, or sometimes some gospel—Kirk Franklin or Tye Tribbett. They don’t really sing; they’re more yelling and stuff, with a choir in the back that’s doing the singing for them. If you’ve ever been to a Black church, it’s kind of that style.

Paris—I just love it. It was the first city that I visited outside of the US, so I think I just always have nostalgia towards that, just realizing how far tennis could take me. It just feels like a home away from home a little bit. People always ask me for Paris recs, but I’m usually just the girl that will just go to the park by herself. I just like the vibe.

Do you have a guilty pleasure or something that you indulge yourself in when you’re away from tennis?

I just started like three weeks ago, but I really enjoy pole dancing. That’s been my thing. I’m one of those people that hobby jumps a lot—I bought a guitar and I haven’t used it; I bought a keyboard—so I need to stop wasting money on stuff that I’m interested in for two weeks. I’m hoping that this one sticks. It’s challenging though—I’m not very great, but one day.

Is there a sport other than tennis that you either watch or play?

I play basketball for fun—I’m not good, I just like it. And I watch American football and basketball—the Dolphins and the Heat—and then track and field when it’s the world championships and the Olympics.

When you’re getting dressed for a big night out, do you have a favorite piece, or something that you love that’s important to you?

I can probably count on my hands the amount of times I’ve went out—in my life—to a bar or club, but I do like to dress up. Sometimes I’ll dress up to just take pictures. Lately I’ve been loving a good heel, because I’m already tall and I just like being taller than people. But also a good bag. I just started working with Miu Miu, so I’ve been experimenting with outfits and stuff with them. They like to do a lot of layering, and layering was something I usually didn’t do because I’m from Florida and it’s hot, but it’s something that I’ve been trying to embrace more. And I love accessories, like a cute bow, or they have the bag charms now—anything to spice up your outfit.

Roland Garros—my first Grand Slam. The whole tournament was just something else. I still remember the emotions to this day. It was the very first tournament where I felt so focused—I could see every little hair on the tennis ball when I was about to hit the shot, and I haven’t ever experienced anything like that before.

Is there a loss this year that was important to you?

Yes—at the US Open when I lost, once again, to Coco Gauff. Coco is a very tough player that I don’t like playing against, but that’s okay. I had two match points—and obviously, with the New York crowd, I get that she would get 95% of the support, and I was actually dealing with that pretty good throughout the whole match. But having two match points to beat her for the first time and to advance to the semifinals of the US Open for the first time—there was a lot on the line that obviously didn’t go my way. That was very, very disappointing for me, and I was sad. But I think with time I’m able to learn from that.

Did you have a hero or a role model when you were growing up?

Yes, my role model was always Roger Federer. To this day I just adore him. For me, he is the best tennis player—not just the way he plays, but what kind of a person he is as well. I just love everything that he does.

I had a very, very quick chat with him at Wimbledon last year. He watched one of my matches and afterward he was there with a lot of other people and I just shook his hand, and he congratulated me and I just said that I’m a big, big fan. But it was very, very, very quick—maybe 20 seconds. But it’s better than nothing, so I’ll take it.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

I’ve actually been talking to my psychologist about this a lot. She told me that if I felt a little bit more calm before the match, maybe I wouldn’t be as nervous. So I have one routine where I listen to motivating, but calm, music—Billie Eilish, Lana Del Rey. Maybe I read a book for a bit. And then before every match, whether I’m calm or if I need a little bit more energy, I watch Roger Federer’s 2017 Australian Open final against Rafa Nadal—five sets, an amazing match. I don’t know how many times I’ve watched it, but I do it to feel the stress of the match, the adrenaline of how they both played. And when I need a little bit more energy, I play Uno with my team. That’s where things get serious—that’s where we can fight a little bit. I also listen to more energetic music—Bon Jovi, Queen. A little bit of older times, but that’s my taste in music.

If you didn’t play any sport, what kind of job would you have?

I’ve been thinking about this a lot recently. For sure I would study more, go to university—but I also think maybe I might want to try acting. I don’t know—my mom says that I’m a pretty good actor when, like, something happens and I need to make it look like I don’t know what’s going on. Maybe I would just give it a shot and see how I would do.

You don’t seem like a stranger to getting dressed up and going out with your friends—

I love to dress up, and maybe a half a year ago I was manifesting heels, because I had never owned high heels in my life. I was talking about high heels everywhere, in every interview, and then I got a high heel from my agent as a gift. But since then, they’ve just been coming at me. Now I have 10 pairs. I don’t wear a super high heel because otherwise I’d break my leg, but I love to put little heels with everything I wear—with jeans, with pants, with a skirt. I think they make the outfit look a little more elegant, and now, for some reason I like the elegant lifestyle.

#6750. The Real-Life Wardrobe of Jamie Campbell Bower, Who Only Wears Suits If They’re McQueen

“I don’t know, I suppose I’m an artist,” Jamie Campbell Bower says with a laugh, after I ask him to describe himself. He’s correct, in more ways than one. If you’ve been consuming pop culture for the last decade and change, it’s less a matter of if you’ve seen the 37-year-old Londoner before, but where. He’s acted in some of the biggest franchises in Hollywood—including Twilight, Harry Potter, The Mortal Instruments, and Stranger Things—while also nurturing a multifaceted music career. As of this month, he’ll be heading to Middle-earth as Celeborn in the third season of Amazon Prime’s epic Lord of the Rings series, The Rings of Power.

During a hectic week of Rings of Power in New York City, Bower and I spent a quiet early morning talking about the bands that helped him find his style as a teenager, the difference between performing as an actor and a musician, and why he loves playing the bad guy.

All clothing and accessories, subject’s own. Coat by MM6 Maison Margiela. Sweater by John Lawrence Sullivan. Vintage skirt. Shoes by John Lawrence Sullivan. Sunglasses by Persol (throughout). Jewelry by Pianegonda.

Jamie Campbell Bower: It’s complexity. With any character, there has to be a level of complexity. Playing in the shadow self is really illuminating, to be Jungian. You have to know it in order for it to not take over. I found it particularly interesting to rationale and reason, even though this character was doing terrible things. I have always found it really interesting to dig away and find the why. So much of that character was really about isolation and pain and not feeling like they had a sense of belonging in the space for them. Obviously, they find this power that gives them this sense of safety. It becomes the wall, and it gives them purpose, and it hides them from the world and from being hurt. What draws me to any character is complexity and understanding the balance. It’s almost anthropological in a way.

It was amazing. I was so terrified on day one. I’m always nervous about joining any show, doing any gig. But I remember day one of actually shooting with other cast members, turning around to Nick Müller, our A-camera operator, and I just went, “Look, Nick, you’ve been here way longer than I have. If I’m in your way, just tell me to fucking move.”

I’d been a part of Twilight as well—joined that on the second movie after watching a cultural moment explode—and I was in that position again with Stranger Things. It was so big. I was joining this new world, but everyone was wicked and super kind. I made some amazing friends. I love Millie [Bobby Brown]. She’s just the best. She’s like my little sister, and also like my big sister at times as well. She’s got so much sage advice and is so brilliant at what she does and so driven. I am in awe of her, and I was from the moment I met her.

I’ve got the hand of Vecna. I took it out on Fallon [the other] night. I told this story, but I got my bag searched in Mexico City on the way in over the weekend. We pulled up and one of the people there looked at me—her eyes got big. She said, “Vecna.” I’ve got three massive fuck-off suitcases. They’re going through them and I’m like, “Look, I’ve got the hand of Vecna in here. Do you want to see it?” And then it ended up being the quickest bag search ever. I got some elf ears with me as well, both made by the same guy, Barrie Gower.

It was the summer when I was 15. I spent it wearing a visor with spiky hair, because I used to skate growing up in super baggy jeans. I remember turning up being like, “That’s not you.” Skating is a part of who I am, but I was looking to represent myself in some way, shape, or form.

Then we started this indie band when I was 16, 17. Devonté Hynes had this band called Test Icicles. I always used to look at those guys with their skinny jeans and their big hair, and I was just like, “That’s a bit of me, that.” How skinny can my jeans get? How drain pipe-y am I? That’s where I really started to find my own identity.

I’ve been fortunate enough throughout my career to meet and work with such beautiful creative people in fashion and find myself more within that, too. I was talking about it to somebody yesterday: When you try a fit on that is not you, it’s like having a bad haircut. You don’t want to do that. I’m even the same if I’m doing a photoshoot. I always go through the rail and I’ll say, “That’s not my vibe. I can’t say that I’m going to wear that.” Of course, I’m always willing to try, I’m always willing to push. But you know yourself better as you get older.

It was from Alexander McQueen. I loved the identity of that brand, but I couldn’t afford a jacket, or a suit, or even a scarf. But the smaller pieces, the rings and the wallets, were like 100 bucks. Those were the things that I would gravitate towards and buy.

More recently, within the last 10 years, I remember coming here to New York for a show that I did called Will, going to Bergdorf, and buying a couple of pairs of Comme des Garçons trousers. As they were being rung up, I was like, “All right.” It wasn’t loads—we’re not talking thousands—but it was still a lot of money. That was probably the first big clothing purchase that I ever made. And I’ve still got the trousers. I used to wear them on stage in the band as well, which is foolish.

Got a bunch of stuff from H. Lorenzo the other day—some great shirts, some great jackets. I really like how they curate the store. My most recent purchase is a lot of stuff from the new Ann Demeulemeester collection. I actually just bought a sick leather trench from it—brown leather, which is fire.

Jacket by Thom Browne. Shirt, jeans, shoes by Ann Demeulemeester.

Going back to when we were kids: Test Icicles, the Libertines, the Rakes, Franz Ferdinand, Editors. Got to meet a few of those guys throughout my travels, which was always pretty sick. Nick Cave. Warren Ellis. Nick has got such a sharp style, as does Warren. Warren’s a bit more unbuttoned. I met Warren in Venice five years ago. He was stood at the end of the pier and I was so excited to meet him, I just bounded up. I was like, “Hi, Mr. Ellis. My name’s Jamie.” And I just blurted out to him for ages, and then I was like, “Thank you so much.” He said, "Good to meet you, mate. Bye.”

I think fluidity and being myself is always the main thing. I’ve never felt wholly comfortable in a regular suit. I remember we were invited to do a show in Venice, and the band that we were in was pretty heavy. We wore suits in an environment that for us felt almost quite subversive. The music that we played didn’t really fit that. I quite enjoyed that.

But on the whole, I don’t love suits too much. I like to keep it more interesting and fluid. I’m not saying that they can’t be interesting for other people, but I’ve never been interested [in them myself]. Apart from McQueen, but that’s because something like the McQueen shoulder is so identifiable and creates such an incredible silhouette. That’s probably the only time I’ve ever really been like, “I can wear this suit for a long time.” But yeah, I avoid anything that doesn’t feel right for me.

It’s hard to say. I do feel like so often they can blend. I’ve been so fortunate in my career, being drawn to things that feel like me and getting to explore different parts of myself on film. That does have an effect on the music that I’m making at the time.

With a film or a television series, you’re saying someone else’s words and building a character, but also at times injecting your own personal experience into that. In music, they are your words. You can make a choice to be like, “I’m going to build a world in this song to express something.” Or I can just be like, “This is me.” So, they can scratch different itches, but I think that they work in symbiosis sometimes.

The original movies came out when I was 12, so they were pretty seminal. I remember being in Hong Kong on a trip when The Hobbit was coming out. I was on my own, and I went to a cinema in a place called Pacific Place to watch it. That made a really big impact on me—it felt like a fantastical world that I could see myself in.

I started auditioning for it in 2024. Walking into it, of course, I was elated. I felt so lucky and so happy, like I was a little kid again. Like, I was 11 or 12 on stage in some provincial town outside of London, and now I get to fuckin’ walk into this Lord of the Rings world and be an elf? Dude, that’s sick.

Three non-negotiable albums that everyone… Oh, bloody Nora!

I discovered Dylan when I was like 16, when we were reading [J. D.] Salinger and Allen Ginsberg and books like On the Road. Let’s go with a classic. Freewheelin’ is old-school enough. It’s cool, pre-him going electric, which I adore as well. Highway 61 Revisited is a great record too. Take your pick between those two. Chopin’s Nocturnes are amazing. That’s a beautiful, beautiful piece to get into. Then there’s Nick Cave. I did an interview before and I chose Murder Ballads, which is a great record. But I also love some of the more recent work, like Ghosteen or Skeleton Tree. Ghosteen is amazing.

Oh, Ghosteen’s wicked. Let’s go with that. I referenced the artwork for Ghosteen on my last release. My album cover was by an artist called Thomas Cole, who did a collection of paintings about the journey from birth to death. He also did paintings of the Garden of Eden. From what I have now seen, those paintings heavily inspired the artist that did the paintings for Ghosteen as well, which is kind of insane.

So, he’s from the East. It’s the swearing.

#6749. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6748. Oven-Roasted Turkey

The perfect Thanksgiving turkey is easier to make than you might think. Whether you're a first-timer planning a Friendsgiving dinner for your closest pals or the one whose house the whole family gathers at year after year, this recipe will help make your turkey the star of the dinner table. Let this be the year you ace Thanksgiving hosting and find your annual go-to guide for everything—roasting time, thawing, the secret to perfectly browned skin—on how to present the perfect roast bird.

Remove the giblets, trussing, and pop-up thermometers from the turkey. Pat the turkey completely dry inside and out with paper towels. If you plan to cut the wishbone out now, face the turkey neck opening toward you and locate the V-shaped wishbone in the neck cavity. With a sharp and flexible boning knife, using a short but firm swiping motion, gently cut the bone from the breast meat by making long incisions on both sides of the bone. Pry the bone loose with a paper towel or clean kitchen towel and discard. Using your fingers, separate the turkey breast from the skin.

In a spice grinder or mortar and pestle, grind all of the spices until they're finely ground and well combined. This will allow the spices to adhere to the surface of the turkey, especially the dried thyme.

Cover the entire turkey with the seasoning mix, turning the turkey over to season the back as well. Be sure to season under the breast skin and in the cavity. Transfer the turkey to a roasting rack. Refrigerate, uncovered, until cold, at least 12 hours and up to 2 days.

Arrange a rack in the lower third of the oven with no rack above it; preheat to 450°. Gently pat the turkey with paper towels to remove any excess moisture. Place the shallot, lemon, garlic, fresh thyme, and sage in the turkey cavity and neck opening. Be sure not to overfill the turkey. Err on the side of not stuffing everything in if it doesn’t fit. The turkey cavity needs airflow to cook evenly, and blocking that airflow will result in a longer cook time and a drier turkey. Drizzle the turkey with oil. Insert a leave-in probe thermometer (if using) into the turkey thigh or breast and transfer the roasting pan to the oven.

Roast the turkey for 30 minutes. Reduce the oven temperature to 350°. Continue to roast until the temperature in the thickest part of the breast registers 155° and the thigh registers 165°, about 1 hour and 30 minutes more, up to 2 hours more, rotating once during cooking to help the skin brown evenly. Let the turkey rest, uncovered, for 45 minutes before carving.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. Leftovers can also be frozen. Chill any carved turkey in the refrigerator until cold, then transfer to a freezer-safe bag or container and label it with the contents and date. Store in the deepest part of the freezer for up to 6 months.

#6747. Sommelier-Approved Thanksgiving Wines

The challenge of picking wine for Thanksgiving is multifaceted. Your selections must be lively enough to enjoy as guests work their way through charcuterie, balanced enough to play well with turkey, and versatile enough to rub shoulders with dessert. It’s a tall order for anyone tasked with bringing the bottles to their holiday meal. To help, five beloved wine-heads from across the country weighed in on the bottles that everyone around your holiday table will adore.

Here are the crowd-pleasing offerings sure to liven up your Thanksgiving.

For Adam Robins, beverage director at State Bird Provisions and The Progress in San Francisco, there’s no better way to start a festive meal than with Champagne. Bérêche & Fils delivers classic brioche notes tempered with fruit like Bosc and Asian pears, brought together with a snap of acidity to prime the palate for the feast ahead

Les Cigales dans la Fourmilière Escarpolette Blanc 2024

Los Angeles’s Lasita is beloved for its natural wine selections and its menu of kicky Filipino favorites. Co-owners Chase and Steff Valencia adore this Languedoc orange wine, which offers notes of bold fruit—peach and apricot—and a bright acidity that can cut through even the butteriest of mashed potatoes.

Peter Lauer Riesling Schonfels Kabinett No. 111

“More people should be drinking Riesling,” says Matt Turner of Lei, one of Bon Appétit’s Best New Restaurants of 2026. He points to this German stunner with direct minerality and notes of stone fruit, which sips just as well alongside a cheesy cauliflower gratinée as a garlic-studded beef tenderloin.

At the James Beard–nominated Wild Child in Lafayette, Louisiana, natural wine rules supreme. Ian LaCour, who helps curate the bottle list, gravitates toward this muscular red. Thanks to a silky body and dusky notes of stewed red fruit, it plays well with the “heartier proteins on the Thanksgiving table.”

You’d be forgiven for being unfamiliar with macvin, a niche style of fortified wine made in France’s Jura region. But the oaky fresh apple and cider notes in this punchy bottling—akin to a less-oxidized, sweeter oloroso sherry—make for a divine digestif. “It fares well with every dessert,” says Nick Arone of Detroit’s Bar Chenin.

#6744. 11 Best Cowboy Boots in 2026, According to GQ Editors

You might think that cowboy boots are a privilege reserved for ranch hands and folks who can actually ride a horse. But with a little chutzpah, the best cowboy boots are just as adept on a saddle as they are on the subway. Is that so surprising? Before they blossomed into their fashionable forms, much of menswear’s most riffed on garments were rooted in function: cargo pants, work jackets, even suits. With enough time, they were adopted by civilians and adapted to their second lives as symbols of self-expression and creativity, not just job uniforms. Cowboy boots are no different.

In terms of styling, the classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with some well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage boot cuts) and with a snap shirt. And that's still a great approach. But if you open up your mind and step outside of the saloon, the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a ‘70s-inspired suit screams filthy rich oil tycoon if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or, why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots. So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

And if you’re having trouble, well, that’s why you’re here. We’ve wrangled together the best cowboy boots west—and east—of the Mississippi, from the budget-friendly to the ostentatious and every vibe in-between.

The good folks at Tecovas are living, breathing proof that direct-to-consumer brands aren’t all operated by algorithms tasked with solving imaginary problems. The DTC upstart might be the youngest of the bootmakers on this list, but it's quickly endeared itself to budget-strapped swashbucklers with a hankering for democratically-priced kicks.

Take, for example, the Cartwright, a handsome riff on a classic western silhouette made in Leon, Mexico, a bona fide cobbling capital of the world with over a century of expertise to draw on. It boasts hand-laid cording at the shaft, a resoleable Goodyear-welt construction, and a slew of colors and leathers to choose from, including genuine cowhide and goat leather. They’re not the cheapest boots on this list, but the relatively approachable price belies the craftsmanship involved. For $375, they’re one small step up from our favorite budget cowboy boots—but one giant leap in overall quality.

You can think of roper boots as the chilled-out version of the average western boot. Originally designed for calf roping, roper boots feature a shorter shaft and a shorter, squared off heel. These details made it easier for cowboys to dismount their horse and run after the calves they roped. Coincidentally, they also make roper boots easier to walk in which is why some people prefer them over other cowboy boots for everyday wear.

Our pick for the best roper boots currently goes to Red Wing. (Perhaps no surprise, given the brand also makes our favorite trend-proof boots.) Part of Red Wing's Heritage line, they're crafted with premium S.B. Foot Tanning Company leather, and feature Goodyear welt construction so you can have them resoled and keep ‘em going for a long time. Plus, if you’re just dipping your toes into the cowboy boot world, the minimalist uppers forgo the decorative western stitching which makes them easier to style.

If you’re after that western look but need a pair of boots that can handle the demands of a jobsite, a lot of guys will tell you to look to Ariat. That’s because they manage to blend classic cowboy style with modern-day features, and a palatable price point in perfect proportion. While they do offer a range of work boots in lace-up styles, their Groundbreaker boots are a standout with classic cowboy boot looks.

They’re made of full-grain leather, include a supportive and comfortable insole, and meet ASTM standards for slip resistance and electrical safety. Because it’s among Ariat’s most popular styles, it’s also available in a wide range of colorways, toe shapes, and even steel toe versions. Some more traditional cowboys will poo-poo the fact that these aren’t made stateside, but if you’re on a budget, you’ll get more than what you pay for.

Cowboy boots aren’t all rough-and-tumble affairs. In fact, the right pair can easily strut the red carpet or waltz into a fancy restaurant with panache. You’ll want a pair with leather that shines up well and in a darker colorway. For date nights and more formal affairs, these Tony Lamas will impress thanks to the exotic lizard skin uppers and low-key embroidery. They’re the kind of boots that can play well for the in-laws with a tailored suit or play a rock-’n’-roll star with some vintage jeans and a tight white tee.

These days, most boot brands walk in the shadows of one brand: Lucchese. They’ve been outfitting American presidents, high-profile celebs, and the Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders for decades and it’s all thanks to their commitment to high-quality craftsmanship. Though any pair of Lucchese’s would earn you more than a few approving head nods, the most coveted are the boots that they make in their Texas workshop.

Using a range of full-grain leathers and exotic leathers like caiman alligator and pirarucu fish skin, each pair is crafted by master bootmakers using time-honored techniques. The Gavin, in their iconic Black Cherry, is a picture-perfect style featuring smooth Santini goat leather uppers with intricate embellishments, welted construction, and lemonwood pegs—made the old-fashioned way, basically. They’ll cost you a pretty penny, of course, but they'll last pretty much forever, and the drip you’ll get in return is priceless.

From Ralph Lauren’s western-inspired sub-label, these RRL boots meld high-end materials with old-world craftsmanship and feature American-tanned leather uppers, Goodyear-welted construction, and vintage-style rubber soles—all crafted in a multi-generational Texas bootmaking factory.

Frye is another American brand with proven boot quality chops. (In fact, it claims to be America's oldest continually-operating boot company.) Its Roper boot has all the same strengths as Red Wing's, and comes in a non-roughout leather.

We don't typically include the same designers twice on one list, but Tecovas are that good. The Johnny is for anyone who wants a softer, slightly more charming boot than the eternal Cartwright up top.

For fellas whose style skews a little more regular-guy than rodeo, these lower-profile, lower-priced Ropers have a Goodyear welt and Vibram outsole. Bang for your, ahem, buck.

Wythe's playing-card-inspired boots feature all the bells and whistles, including premium leather inside and out, hand-applied details, lemonwood pegs, and second-to-none construction all-around. While some brands tap the expert bootmakers in Léon, Mexico to pump out high-quality mass-appeal boots, Wythe tapped these artisans to really let them cook.

All of Yuketen's shoes are perfect, which is a big part of the reason Drake's now carries them. And while they're best known for their moccasin styles, the brand makes an exceptionally handsome cowboy boot too. Really, they're just showing off now.

The classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage bootcuts) and a snap-button shirt. But open up your mind and step outside of the saloon and the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a '70s-inspired suit screams filthy-rich oil tycoon—if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots (though you certainly can). So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

Peter Middleton knows a thing or two about the lifestyle having cut his teeth at Ralph Lauren and used it as a springboard for his own western-inspired brand, Wythe. “To me the beauty and shape of the Cowboy Boot (and a lot of the original design intent) lies in its curves and that’s what makes a great boot SEXY. There isn't a lot of men's footwear that has these dramatic curves, leather, and a high heel but the right cowboy boot has them all.”

He says that good cowboy boots should be made with natural leathers that age well with wear, mould to the wearer’s feet, and can be recrafted repeatedly. His non-negotiables include full leather construction from the insole to the outsole, linings, uppers, and heels. Look for Goodyear welted construction which will allow you to have the boots resoled and extend their life. The toe bug (the fancy stitching at the toe), should sit right where your foot flexes to help cover up the crease that comes with each step. Preferably, this would be corded by hand, of course.

Price points will vary, and you can get some well-made boots for around $300. The really great stuff will often be twice that much. Middleton says, “the best thing to do is wait and save up until you can buy the version you actually want because its impossible to cut corners and still deliver the product you want.” So if you can be patient, save up. If you can’t, try buying secondhand. But if you simply can’t wait, you’ll do well enough with plenty of the mid-tier brands until you’re ready to upgrade.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you.

#6743. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6741. We Tried Every Boxed Stuffing We Could Find—These Are The Only Ones We’d Buy Again

Some mixes taste so homemade, they just might fool your Thanksgiving guests.

In my opinion, stuffing is the crème de la crème of a Thanksgiving feast. I’d choose it over any other carb or veggie side. Everyone knows stuffing balances a buttery, crispy top with a moist, tender interior and subtle aromatics. It should be the greatest complement to a turkey. But sometimes we can’t get around to making a homemade stuffing on Thanksgiving, so we settle for a box mix.

We tried a variety of stuffings so you don’t have to wonder which one to pick up at the grocery store. We were looking for stuffing that could be mistaken for homemade, with a balanced texture and real seasoning. We tried eight stuffings, but only five were worthy of adding to your holiday table or weeknight rotation.

This ShopRite stuffing is super weeknight-friendly, and I wouldn’t hesitate to make this for an easy dinner side. Because it’s made with chicken broth, you can use water to make it without losing too much flavor.

This Pepperidge Farm Stuffing was the most surprising one I tried. Because it contains whole wheat and therefore is a little darker in color, I wasn’t sure I would like it. The flavor was excellent, though, and I really appreciated the homemade feel of having to add your own fresh chopped onion and celery.

It's admittedly been years since I had my end-all, be-all favorite boxed stuffing as a kid, Stovetop’s Savory Herbs. And you know what? It really holds up.

As the name suggests, this boxed stuffing mix is Big-S Savory and loaded with herbs, with a buttery, peppery backbone. It gets perfectly crispy around the edges. It’s both nostalgic-good and delicious enough to keep a box on hand for after Turkey Day, if not just to make these sausage stuffing bites.

Here is where the fooling comes in, with Kinder's Brown Butter & Herbs Stuffing Mix. One bite of this garlicky, nutty stuffing had me say out loud, “Oh, this is deluxe.”

Not only that, but this might be the easiest stuffing of them all, with no fewer than three different ways to prepare and serve it. There’s a sausage-spiked version, a skillet-made version, and an ultra-savory version with leeks. In short, if you're really in the mood for a homemade stuffing experience, but you're running out of prep time, Kinder's stuffing will trick everyone into thinking you made this fully on your own.

While Kinder’s is great when you still want to eat like a Thanksgiving maximalist, some of us want the easiest (but no less delicious) route. In which case, Mrs. Cubbison’s Traditional Stuffing will take you there.

I’ve long been a fan of the brand’s herby, buttery croutons, so I’m not surprised that Mrs. Cubbison’s Traditional Stuffing is yet another one of its products I'll always keep on hand. The bread base is just the right amount of toasted and caramelized, making for a stuffing that's tender and crispy around the edges (no mush here). Plus, it'll even free up some space in your oven since it can be made in the slow cooker, too.

#6740. Mamdani and Hochul Visit Queens Night Market to Get Out the Vote

Zohran Mamdani wanted to share with the governor, but the vendor at the Taiwanese Yummy tent wasn’t having it. Cheng Liu insisted the New York mayor try his own bowl of beef noodle soup—the chef’s way.

Instead of trying a bite from Governor Kathy Hochul, Mamdani watched and waited as Liu arranged slippery, wide noodles underneath pickled mustard greens, herbs, and slices of succulent brisket that had been cooked for eight hours, all ladled with a delicate broth. Mamdami started to dig in with his chopsticks when Liu rushed over to spoon in a generous amount of homemade chili oil.

“The mayor is not scared of spicy food,” Liu said via his son’s translation. “We wanted to give him Taiwanese cuisine.”

At the Queens Night Market, Mamdani and Hochul struck an unusual pair: a New York mayor and governor who get along.

Three days before Election Day, the political allies arrived at Flushing Meadows Corona Park in a motorcade of black SUVs to pose for photos and get out the vote for the Democratic party. Hochul has made the city part of her final push in a reelection campaign against Republican Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive endorsed by President Donald Trump.

In a joint interview with Hochul, Mamdani told Bon Appétit that he was showing up for the governor because she was showing up for immigrant New Yorkers. Earlier this year, Hochul signed legislation to ban local and state law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration operations, and to stop police at all levels from covering their face when interacting with the public.

“The governor has stood up and called for public safety to actually be public safety and not just be an assistance and an accompaniment of ICE,” Mamdani said. “That has been part of what makes people feel like they can be part of this city.”

The mayor also mentioned that the Queens Night Market was a favorite with constituents because of the price. Every dish is capped at $6. Hochul, running on affordability, points to her expansion of free school lunch statewide. “As a mom, this is personal,” she said. “I made a lot of peanut butter and jelly sandwiches over the years for kids.”

Representing different generations and factions of their party, Mamdani and Hochul recognize what they stand to gain together. Mamdani needed Hochul to expand free childcare and greenlight plans for a second-home tax. Hochul needs the enthusiasm of the Democratic Socialist mayor’s voting bloc.

Hochul said she and Mamdani are aligned on lowering the cost of living and supporting the small business owners that make the food and nightlife scene so special.

“It’s a rare day in New York for this kind of relationship,” Hochul said, “but when we talk to each other, we don’t disagree on these issues.”

The pair of politicians approached the night market in a coordinated operation that included advance teams, extra security, and business casual ’fits: Hochul in jeans, Mamdani tie-less in a quarter-zip. The mayor—who has made his appetite a key part of his public identity—appeared less stiff in his interactions with food vendors, but Hochul gamely grabbed chopsticks and posed for selfies.

John Wang, who launched the Queens Night Market in 2015, said politicians are a regular presence here. “Every election season, they come out,” Wang said. “Even if they’ve never been here before, they’re like, ‘Yeahhh! I love the Queens Night Market.’” He said some (2020 presidential candidate Andrew Yang, for instance) get feted like Mamdani, and others (N.Y. Sen. Chuck Schumer) draw a tamer response. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez used to come a lot, Wang said, and would always get swarmed by supporters.

For the last market of the season, which fell on Halloween, Mamdani might as well have been a member of BTS. Vendors and visitors alike stared slackjawed, squealed, and uttered “oh my God!”

A young man named Asad showed up in a Mamdani costume with no idea he would meet the mayor, let alone pose for photos that brought him to tears.“This is Bruce Blakeman’s nightmare!” the mayor said of his Mamdani double.

“It was surreal, emotional a little bit,” said Asad, who declined to share his last name. Asad said he was born in Karachi, Pakistan, became a U.S. citizen in 2022, and voted for Mamdani after moving to New York from Florida.

At the Ella Spice stand, Akera Phillip represents Grenada with breadfruit croquettes, fried cou-cou, and to-go pouches of sorrel. Phillip, who named her business after her grandmother, felt “elated” and “blessed” to serve her food to the leaders of the state and the city.

“As a small island girl, it just made me feel big,” she said.

Akera Phillip holds breadfruit croquettes.

At the Epis by Steve tent, Hochul told Steve Lahens she could handle “Buffalo spicy,” a nod to her hometown, rather than admit to any trouble with his Haitian pikliz. Lahens and his wife fixed up plates of griot (fried pork) with diri djondjon (black rice) and makawoni au graten, a Caribbean mac and cheese he makes with bell peppers, “evaporated milk and a few little things I can’t talk about.”

Lahens said he was born in Haiti but came to the U.S. in 1988. A workplace injury pushed him toward cooking, “and it changed my life, for the better.” He began cooking out of his house but now works out of the Mangrove shared kitchen at the Flatbush Central Caribbean Marketplace. He was excited to hobnob with the governor and the mayor, but Lahens also said New York small businesses need more help.

“The rent could be lower so people like me could get a spot,” Lahens said. “Right now I’m stuck in catering. I love it, too, but my whole plan and goal is to get a storefront.”

#6738. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6737. We Tried Starbucks’ All-New Holiday Drinks—Here’s What We’d Order Again

I don’t care whether your annual traditions call for the start of the Christmas season on November 1 or you’re a total Scrooge until after Thanksgiving, Starbucks’ holiday menu is officially here—which means it’s time to retire the Pumpkin Spice Lattes (for now) and embrace your holly-er, jollier alter ego.

Naturally, I had to get my hands on the new flavors—and reacquaint myself with the classics—in the name of journalism and the holiday spirit! From the dessert-inspired tiramisu drinks to the light and bright Refreshers (there are two, by the way!), I put Starbucks’ latest creations to the test. Here’s which ones I’d order again—and what I’d skip.

If you want your coffee to taste like a straight-up dessert, good news: I found the morning pick-me-up for you. Starbucks has created the ultimate holiday treat in this Tiramisu Velvet Latte. Inspired by the classic Italian treat, the new signature drink combines espresso, milk, and vanilla syrup with a fluffy Velvet Mascarpone Cold Foam and cocoa dusting that mimics the OG. It’s sweet without being overly sweet, and the cold foam adds a rich, creamy layer like the actual dessert. Whether you get it hot or iced, it’s a fun departure from your typical Peppermint Mocha order.

Cold brew purists, this one’s for you. Starbucks is also giving its classic Cold Brew a holiday makeover with the same formula as its latte: vanilla syrup, Velvet Mascarpone Cold Foam, and a dusting of cocoa and coffee. Unlike the latte, this format allows the coffee to do more of the talking, and the creamy mascarpone foam adds just a touch of dessert energy.

Now, there are actually two ways to try the refresher: the classic version, a.k.a. the Apple Pomegranate Refresher, with crisp apple flavors and popping pomegranate-flavored pearls; and the Snowy Apple Drink, which features the same ingredients with coconut milk for a creamier take.

The classic refresher is definitely brighter and fruitier, with a tart-sweet apple flavor and sugary pops of pomegranate, while the Snowy Apple Drink is more mellowed out thanks to the coconut milk. The result still captures the key flavors, but delivers them with a smoother, creamier finish.

You can customize the refreshers even more by adding a citrusy twist of lemonade or adjusting the caffeine levels—anywhere from no caffeine to light caffeine to full-blown Energy Refresher.

While I genuinely enjoyed trying all three new beverages, I probably wouldn’t order the Tiramisu Velvet Latte again—but that’s only because the Tiramisu Velvet Cold Brew exists. I’m always going to gravitate toward a more coffee-forward drink. And as for the Apple Pomegranate Refreshers, they’re a fun addition to the lineup—light, fruity, and the perfect pick-me-up for after a long day of Christmas shopping (especially if you add the caffeine boost).

#6736. Going Home—A Day in the Life With Libby Taverner As She Walks the Chanel Show in Sydney

One of Australia’s buzziest models, Libby Taverner made her runway debut during the fall 2025 season. Since then, her career has been a frenetic blur. For spring 2027, she walked no fewer than 27 shows, Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel among them. When the storied French house decided to reprise its resort 2027 show in Sydney, it was no surprise the 20-year-old was given a ring.

The Sydney show not only marked a significant moment for Chanel—it was their first Australian outing since 1982—but also for the young model. “It’s still relatively early in my journey of living overseas. Being able to come home and walk a Chanel show in Australia feels incredibly special, and it’s an opportunity that I honestly didn’t imagine would come around so soon,” she told Vogue.

“There’s just a little sparkle in my heart knowing that I’m doing something so incredible in my home country. It makes me feel really proud,” she added.

For Taverner, the show meant that she could serve as a guide to her fellow model friends and industry peers, many of whom were experiencing their first times Down Under. Lucky for them, Taverner considers herself an expert at all things Australia, as she grew up in multiple parts of the country. “I was born in Gladstone, Queensland, before my family decided to travel around Australia,” she says. “We spent a couple of years in Perth and Bundaberg too.”

Her top Sydney recommendation? Hitting the Australian coastline. “There’s something for everyone, whether you want to swim, surf, or go for a coastal walk, or simply spend some time relaxing in the sun.” Catching the sunset at the beach with some fish and chips or and a pitstop at Yo-Chi for some fro-yo are must-dos too. “It’s such a simple thing, but to me it’s a very quintessential Australian experience.”

But most importantly for those wanting the full Aussie experience, Taverner recommends taking a step back and slowing down. “The best way to experience Australia is to slow down, explore a little, and embrace that relaxed outdoor lifestyle that we’re so lucky to have.”

Below, a day in the life of Libby Taverner as she gets ready to walk the Chanel resort 2027 reprise show in Sydney.

Fashion week is always such an exciting whirlwind, with everyone traveling from different parts of the world and moving from one city to the next. But there’s something different about walking in Sydney. It feels a little more personal, and I think there’s an added sense of gratitude because I get to experience this moment somewhere that means so much to me. It’s a feeling I don't think I’ll forget anytime soon.

#6735. 18 Best Raincoats for Men 2026, According to GQ Editors

Decades ago, your only options for rainy weather coverage were some kind of trench coat, a coarse wool overcoat, or, if you really needed to be out in it, a thick rubber sack that kept you dry but didn’t breathe. Thankfully, material science has advanced.

There are, of course, umbrellas? And we won’t stop you looking into those. But ask anyone from the Pacific Northwest, and they’ll tell you their rain jacket does all that work with ease. That’s because raincoats aren’t an accessory to your outfit: they’re the main focus. A good raincoat can turn your sad ensemble into head-turning Paparazzi fodder, or at the very least, keep you dry and stylish when it’s wet out.

Still not convinced? We figured—so we tested the best rain jackets and coats for men on the market right now, from the tried-and-true natural-fabric mainstays to the buzzy, newfangled riffs, and everything in between. Here they are.

Arc'teryx's Beta LT jacket is the pinnacle of no-BS rain defense, beloved by wannabe Everest climbers, GQ Recommends editors, and meme-savvy TikTokers alike. Its custom Gore-Tex fabrication will keep you from getting soaked during the harshest of downpours, while its breathable pores work overtime to let water vapor (a.k.a. sweat) escape. That sleek, streamlined silhouette also lends itself naturally to a range of pairings, from straight-fit jeans and sneakers to a full-on “Scaling Kilimanjaro” kit—cargos, backpack, hiking boots—perfect for all of your wildcard outdoor activities.

It’s an investment, but hundreds of guys were showering in theirs for a reason: If you need top-tier weather protection and long-term durability—and are willing to invest—this is still the best rain jacket for serious outdoor use. That said, most dudes chasing the clout that Arc’teryx affords won’t need to max out its capabilities. Still, it’s good to know that if you’re ever caught in a downpour that won’t let up, the Beta’s the one waterproof jacket that won’t leave you high and, uh, wet.

When it comes to outdoor gear that keeps up with Mother Nature, Patagonia’s among the first to come to mind. The OG gorpcore label has more than its fair share of bangers for every climate from the iconic Baggies shorts to its range of plush fleece jackets, and when it comes to rainy weather, there’s the Torrentshell jacket. It’s a canonical piece of kit for Patagonia and has kept customers dry and fly for years.

The latest version features a three-layer shell system that maximizes water-repellency and breathability with a 100% recycled nylon face fabric. It features toasty microfleece-lined handwarmer pockets, welted zippers for water protection (plus pit zips for ventilation), and the entire thing can pack down into itself. So pack it up, throw it in your bag, and bust it out whenever the weather turns out to be worse than what the weatherman says. With a feature set like that, you’d expect to pay through the nose, but we’re thrilled to say that it doesn’t even break $200.

The advancements in rain-wicking technology tickles our lizard brains as much as watching a rock-crushing machine turn a boulder into pebbles. But as much as we appreciate multi-layered DWR-coated materials and heat-sealed seams give us joy, we also have a great reverence and appreciation for rain coats of yore. Enter the waxed jacket, a time-tested fabric used by sailors off the British coast since the 1800s.

If you’re gonna get a waxed jacket, you’d best get a Barbour, the reigning champ of waxed jackets. Barbour has more options and collaborations than ever, so it can be tricky to get your head around what’s what but for our money, the classic Beaufort is the Goldilocks of wax jackets. Where the Bedale is shorter and styles like the Border run down to the mid-thigh, the Beaufort is just right but still long enough to layer over your sport coats. Whichever you choose, don’t forget to re-wax at home after a few seasons. Guys seem to be nervous to do it, but it’s easy, and everytime I’ve re-waxed mine, people compliment me on how great it looks. The reward for your grunt work is a jacket you'll keep for decades to come.

This season, J.Press has unearthed a Rare Barbour: the Burghley. It hasn’t been in the brand’s regular rotation for a number of years, earning it a following among collectors in places like Japan. But now it’s back in all its sweeping, full-length glory.

Originally designed to extend past the knees (and over the saddle and tops of riding boots) the Burghley protects the rider from rain and thorns. It’s a dramatic silhouette that will set you apart from all the cropped Transport and Bedales out there. Sure, it has equestrian heritage, but you needn’t be keeping a stable to wear one. It’s a great alternative to a trench, at home in the city as well as the country. And yes, it’s still made in England.

The perfect trench coat does exist, and Burberry, inventor of the style's signature gabardine fabric in 1879, cracked the code on it long ago. In the nearly 150 years since, surprisingly little has changed about the silhouette, and for good reason. The classic fit means it's roomy enough to layer over your slouchiest Armani-inspired suiting, while the belted design gives it instant sophistication. Plus, the lining and under-collar check pattern is unmistakably Burberry—an investment-worthy flex since the coat was invented.

Its WWI heritage is well-documented—British officers wore it in the trenches, using details like the shoulder flap for rifle recoil and belt rings for canteens and grenades serving real military functions. Today, it’s less about battlefield utility and more about how that water-resistant cotton gabardine will keep you dry in light city rain. I like the black, but the classic tan is always an option for you too.

Another entry from Vancouver—what can we say, they know a few things about rain up there. Indie label James Coward sources fabric from mills known for their quality and considered production practices, then makes its garments locally in its workshop. This coat is cut from the brand’s durable, waterproof ‘Mastershield cloth, a dense weave that offers protection from the elements. A generous silhouette and roomy raglan sleeves give it natural gravitas in gloomy weather, all while keeping the look relaxed and easy to layer.

Whereas the Arc’teryx Beta is the brand’s versatile all-mountain shell, the Alpha SV is built for technical climbing and severe weather. A helmet-compatible hood, harness-ready chest pockets and pit zips make it the top dog of storm shells.

HAVEN puts a GORPcore spin on the refined, city-ready trench made from three-layer GORE-TEX PRO, a more rugged fabric typically found in shells for climbing and backcountry skiing. It’s serious storm gear with a city sensibility, ready to make you feel invincible during a rainy commute.

The wrap coat is Lemaire’s runaway hit. But this Ventile-cotton style is a rainy-day flex: densely woven, breathable cotton that swells when wet to help keep wind and rain out, without synthetic fibres or coatings. Chic.

Menswear can get a little obsessive about fabric specs and provenance. But when a jacket is this cool, you get why. 100 percent Giza cotton, woven at maximum density in Saitama, Japan and originally developed for the British Air Force and later recommissioned by Japan’s Coast Guard. Yeah, that’s the good stuff.

Prep never left, but J.Press is certainly on its way back. The label’s updated take on a classic hooded parka keeps the familiar military shape sans PFAS with natural Ventile cotton. Choose classic army green, or eye-popping orange.

Haider Ackermann's take on Canada Goose is coming into focus. The brand’s Snow Goose sub-label is more Milan than Manitoba, trading logo-heavy designs for cool colours and modern silhouettes that go well beyond down parkas.

Making a good rain jacket might not take a degree in nuclear science, but Outdoor Research’s founder was actually a nuclear physicist turned avid mountaineer. This stripped-back shell sheds weight and packs small without skimping on protection. Stash it and forget it.

Marmot, meanwhile didn’t pull back on features to shave weight. This soft, quiet waterproof shell is built for movement, with an “Angel-Wing” design that lets you reach overhead without the hem riding up and putting your backside on display.

Reigning Champ has also gone well beyond sweats and tees. This workhorse of a rain jacket is more downtown than summit in style but still meets the moment with GORE-TEX construction and a very digestible price.

Italian fabric. Fifth-generation Portuguese construction. New York City design. That’s the mix behind Knickerbocker’s full-length trench. Its tightly woven, water-repellent fabric helps keep rain out all with the kind of easy, downtown cool Knickerbocker does so well.

Uniqlo’s even more affordable sister brand, GU, delivers a lot of jacket for the money The throwback piping and punchy colours nod to the ’90s, while the water- and wind-resistant fabric makes it practical, too.

A waxed Harrington probably isn’t for a downpour unless your trousers are waxed, too, but it’s ideal for breezy, drizzly, and sunny fall days alike. And, aye, the waxed fabric comes straight from Scotland. No messing about.

Who wants to drag a sopping wet umbrella around only to forget it at the restaurant or in the back of a cab? When you’ve got a trench coat with your cell and headphones in the pockets, it’s almost impossible to lose. Through light mists, heavy rain, and even torrential downpours, the best rain coats are, ironically, the drippiest too. They’ll prevent you from showing up to the function like a poor wet dog and instead make your arrival a warm, dry welcome.

Trench coats that aren’t the only coats vying to shield you from the rain, though. Gorpcore’s popularity has given us waves of tech-y jackets, parkas, and anoraks all wrought from futuristic multi-layered materials that balance breathability with waterproof ability. The result is a cementing of this 21st century sportswear into must-have menswear. And let’s not forget the workwear-adjacent waxed jackets born from sailing the Scottish seas in 15th-century Scotland. With their rugged good looks and a lust for patina, they’ve become stylish staples when the weather’s all doom and gloom.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

I usually whip up a batch of Priya Krishna’s 2019 version the weekend before and feel an outsized sense of pride that I’ve managed to tick one thing off the long prep list. Her recipe is a great starting (or ending) point, but you can jazz it up with a cinnamon stick, star anise, or a few cranks of black pepper if you’d like. Or sub in brown sugar for white—the choice is yours!

You can bake them ahead of time, let them cool, and keep them in the freezer for reheating. Or, if you’re feeling a little adventurous, try their distant cousin, Salt Bread, for even more oohs and ahhs.

Is it even Thanksgiving without pumpkin pie? Rick Martinez’s 2016 rendition is as classic as they come, and it tastes even better the next day (if you’re lucky enough to have any leftovers… come to think of it, maybe just plan on making two?).
